case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The court decided standing, not the outer definition of authorship, and it addressed an animal rather than a system a human directs. It answers who cannot own a work, not who does.
case.holding: A crested macaque that took photographs of itself lacked statutory standing under the Copyright Act, because the Act's terms presume human authors and next-of-kin, and a non-human cannot sue for infringement of works it created.

live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The monkey-selfie case is the closest appellate authority that a non-human creator has no rights in what it makes. It is cited to establish that model outputs have no author of their own, which cuts for AI companies when they disclaim ownership and against anyone trying to anchor rights in the machine itself.

reading.body:
The clearest appellate rule available on non-human authorship is that a non-human cannot sue under the Copyright Act, because the statute presumes human authors and human next-of-kin.

The Ninth Circuit reached that conclusion in 2018 when a wildlife photographer's company was sued on behalf of a crested macaque that had taken photographs of itself. The court resolved the case on standing, meaning it decided only who may bring an infringement claim, not the full definition of who or what qualifies as an author. That distinction matters: the holding answers who cannot own a work, not whether a work made without a human author is protectable at all.

AI disputes cite this case because it is the closest appellate authority for the proposition that model outputs have no author of their own. That framing cuts two ways. AI companies invoke it to disclaim ownership of outputs, which limits their liability exposure. Parties who want to assert rights in machine-generated material find this precedent an obstacle, because it gives no foothold for anchoring rights in the system itself. One live case connected to this area, involving the University of Tennessee Research Foundation and Anthropic, remains active as of the verified date. The data covers standing doctrine and authorship; it does not address training data, licensing, or the power and infrastructure questions that sit upstream of model outputs.
